title: The coat and the dreams (Genesis 37:1–11)
hook: a favorite son, a colored coat, and brothers who can't speak peaceably

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting Esau: the wronged brother ran first. Your line was he ran to meet him. Today, the next generation, and the trouble starts again.

Some family albums have one: the kid in the middle of every picture. The one whose drawings went on the fridge, whose birthday got the bigger cake, who got away with things. A sibling can still name that kid, years later. Genesis has watched this pattern before. Isaac loved Esau more. Rebecca loved Jacob more. Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. Now Jacob, old, called Israel, has twelve sons, and he doesn't even try to hide his favorite.
screen: `THE KID IN EVERY PICTURE.` → `A FAMILY OF FAVORITES.` → `TWELVE SONS, ONE FAVORITE.`

segments.voice: First, the favorite. Joseph is seventeen, the son of Rachel, the wife Jacob loved, born in Jacob's old age. He tends the flocks with his older half-brothers and brings his father a bad report about them. Then the coat. In the Douay-Rheims: "Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him." Could not speak peaceably. Not even hello. Honestly, nobody is sure what that coat looked like. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, gives it many colors. Some readers take the Hebrew, ketonet passim, as a long robe, the kind the second book of Samuel says a king's daughters wore. Either way, it wasn't work clothes. It said: this one doesn't do what you do. Then the dreams. Joseph dreams that his brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. Then that the sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them, both times. The brothers hate him more. Even his father rebukes him: are your mother and I and your brothers to bow down to you? Last, the quiet line. The brothers envied him, Genesis says, but his father kept the matter in mind. Catholics may hear an echo in Luke, where Mary keeps things and ponders them in her heart. The father who caused the trouble also senses something in it he can't yet see.
screen: `SEVENTEEN, AND THE FAVORITE.` · `A COAT THAT SAID: NOT LIKE YOU.` · `SHEAVES AND STARS BOW DOWN.` · `HIS FATHER KEPT THE MATTER.` · then, large: `COULD NOT SPEAK PEACEABLY TO HIM.`

segments.voice: Think through the places you spend time, your family, your work, your parish, your friends, and notice where someone is treated as the favorite and someone else as the afterthought, without rushing to blame anyone. Then look honestly at yourself: is there anyone you favor without meaning to, or anyone you overlook? If you pray, ask for a fairer heart.
Ketonet passim, Joseph's coat of many colors, the robe that said he didn't do what his brothers did, and set off their hatred. Today's word.
Your line: the coat caused trouble. A gift can say more than the giver means. Day three hundred sixty, done.

howItsDone: The Church reads the Joseph story in the weekday Mass during Lent, setting the brothers' envy beside the plot against Jesus in the Gospel.

chat.says: Why did Joseph's brothers hate him so much?
options: Jacob made him the favorite, gave him the coat, and he told his dreams.
He stole their father's blessing by dressing up as one of them.
He'd been raised away from them and came home acting like a prince.
chat.meaning: Jacob loved Joseph above all his sons and made him the coat; then Joseph told dreams of his brothers bowing, and they hated him more.

ketonet passim.meaning: Hebrew for Joseph's coat: many colors, or a long robe

Rachel.meaning: the wife Jacob loved, Joseph's mother

sheaves.meaning: bundles of cut grain stalks tied together

Douay-Rheims.meaning: an old Catholic English translation of the Bible

sources.quoted: Now Israel loved Joseph above all his sons, because he had him in his old age: and he made him a coat of divers colours. And his brethren seeing that he was loved by his father, more than all his sons, hated him, and could not speak peaceably to him.

notes: Douay-Rheims Genesis 37:3–4 quoted from memory ('colours' is the translation's spelling inside the quotation); confirm wording.

Coat: Septuagint chitona poikilon, Vulgate tunicam polymitam (many colors); Hebrew ketonet passim possibly 'long-sleeved' or 'ankle-length'; same phrase in 2 Samuel 13:18 (Tamar). Confirm. The index's 'colored coat' is kept in the hook.

37:10 rebuke paraphrased; 37:11 'his father kept the matter in mind' paraphrased (Douay-Rheims: 'his father considered the thing with himself'). The Luke 2:19 echo is offered as something Catholics 'may hear', not as the text's intent. Confirm.
The outline's practice spelling 'favouritism' is written as 'favoritism' (American spelling).
howItsDone: Genesis 37:3–4, 12–13a, 17b–28 is read on Friday of the Second Week of Lent with the parable of the wicked tenants. Confirm.
